matching_criterion: Acute urticaria (acute spontaneous urticaria, wheals for less than 6 weeks). Any wording that names acute urticaria / hives counts as correct; allergic drug reaction, anaphylaxis or urticarial vasculitis as the final diagnosis does not, unless urticaria is also named.

management_reference.management: First-line treatment is a standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine.
management_reference.source_quote: We recommend a 2nd generation H1-antihistamine as first-line treatment for all types of urticaria

management_reference.management: No routine diagnostic tests in acute spontaneous urticaria.
management_reference.source_quote: We recommend against routine diagnostic measures in acute spontaneous urticaria

management_reference.management: Do not use first-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamines.
management_reference.source_quote: it is strongly recommended not to use 1st generation H1-antihistamines any longer in allergy for adults and especially not for children

management_reference.management: Ask about NSAID intake, including on-demand use, and advise avoiding NSAIDs in patients whose urticaria they trigger.
management_reference.source_quote: Physicians should therefore ask patients about the intake of NSAIDs, including on-demand use, and advise patients with a history to NSAID-induced urticaria to avoid these drugs

management_scoring_note: Only items with a verified source quote are scored; general good practice that the article does not state is not scored.
